> ## How to use this worksheet
>
> **How today runs:** we work in **stages**. I lecture one part, then you stop and write the code for the matching worksheet part, then we go on to the next. Each part below says which lecture part it follows, so you can always find your place — and if you fall behind, the worksheet stands on its own.
>
> Work through each part in order, at your own pace. Type every line of code yourself into a **plain R script** — do not copy-paste. Blocks marked **▶ Run this** are code you should type and execute. Blocks marked **✏️ Your turn** ask you to write, modify, or answer something. Boxes marked **🚀 If you finish early** are optional bonus material.
>
> **Every grey `r` box below is code you type into an R script — not into the Console.** Before you start: **File → New File → R Script**, and save it as `04_graphing_effectively.R` in your project's `scripts/` folder. Then work down the worksheet, adding each block to the bottom of that one script, in order.
>
> **Type the `# ── Part …` header comment at the top of each block, too.** Those comment lines are not decoration — they are how your script stays navigable, how you find your way back to a block that broke, and how I find your work when I read your script. A block with no header comment is a block I cannot place. In RStudio they also show up in the document outline (the `≡` button at the bottom-left of the editor) so you can jump straight to any part.

::: callout-important
## Column names in `pine_data.csv` / `pine_data.xlsx`

Both files hold the **same six columns, with exactly these names**. Type them
exactly as written — R is case-sensitive, and `Needle_Length` or `needle_length`
will not work:

| Column             | What it is                                     |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `source_file`      | the raw team file the row came from             |
| `team`             | field team — one team = **one tree**            |
| `replicate`        | needle number within a tree side (1-8)          |
| `side`             | sun exposure — `"shady"` or `"sunny"`           |
| `needle_length_mm` | needle length, millimetres                      |
| `needle_width_mm`  | needle width, millimetres                       |

After you read the file in, run `names(pine_df)` and check the names on your
screen against this table before you write any other code.
:::

# Part 1 · Load the data

*Follows Lecture Part 1 — the `ggplot` grammar.*

**▶ Run this in your Script:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.1 · Load the data ────────────────────────────────────────────

pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")
```

# Part 2 · Boxplot, from scratch

*Follows Lecture Part 2 — boxplot anatomy.*

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 (Displaying Data) on Canvas, and [R4DS §9 — Layers](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers.html).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 2.1 · Boxplot, from scratch ────────────────────────────────────
pine_box_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)", fill = "Side"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_box_plot
```

# Part 3c · Axis limits with `coord_cartesian()`

*Follows Lecture Part 2c — `coord_cartesian()`.*

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §11.4 — Scales](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/communication.html#scales).

`ggplot` picks the axis range from your data. That is fine while you explore, and
wrong the moment a reader has to judge **how big** a difference is. Set the limits
on purpose.

**▶ Run this in your Script:**

``` r
# ── Part 3c.1 · Axis limits with coord_cartesian() ──────────────────────
# Start the y-axis at zero so the difference is shown at its real size
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 25)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**▶ Run this — both axes at once, on two continuous variables:**

``` r
# ── Part 3c.2 · Axis limits with coord_cartesian() ──────────────────────
pine_scatter_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm, y = needle_width_mm,
                                         color = side)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Width vs. Length",
    x = "Needle length (mm)",
    y = "Needle width (mm)",
    color = "Side"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(5, 25), ylim = c(0.4, 1.8)) +
  theme_minimal()

pine_scatter_plot
```

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ The trap we just saw on screen — use `coord_cartesian()`, not `ylim()`**

`ylim(14, 16)` and `scale_y_continuous(limits = c(14, 16))` **filter your data
before the geom draws it**. Every row outside the range is dropped, and the median,
quartiles, and whiskers are recomputed from what survives — behind a "removed rows"
warning that is very easy to read past.

`coord_cartesian()` computes the statistics on **all** the data and then zooms the
view. The boxes do not move.

**The rule:** `coord_cartesian()` to zoom, `filter()` when you actually mean to
remove data — on purpose, in the data step, where you can see it.
:::

# Part 4 · Map a third variable with color

*Follows Lecture Part 3 — mapping color by group.*

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §9.1 — Aesthetic mappings](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers.html#aesthetic-mappings).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4.1 · Map a third variable with color ──────────────────────────
pine_team_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = team)) +
  geom_point(

    size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8

  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)", color = "Field team") +
```

# Part 4b · Histograms and density curves

*Follows Lecture Part 3b — histograms and density.*

::: callout-tip
**⏱ If we run short in class, finish this part on your own** — nothing later in the worksheet depends on it.
:::

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 on frequency distributions and bin width; [R4DS §10.3 — Variation](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/EDA.html#variation).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4b.1 · Histograms and density curves ───────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "darkblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Needle Length", x = "Needle length (mm)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

``` r
# ── Part 4b.3 · Histograms and density curves ───────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
```

# Part 5 · Mean ± SE, plotted directly

*Follows Lecture Part 4 — mean ± SE with `stat_summary()`.*

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 4 (Estimating with Uncertainty) — what an error bar actually claims; Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 6 on why independence decides which rows you may average.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 5.1 · Mean ± SE, plotted directly ──────────────────────────────
pine_mean_se_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15),
    alpha = 0.3, size = 2
  ) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.15) +
  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_mean_se_plot
```

# Part 7b · A themes file you write once and `source()` forever

*Follows Lecture Part 6 — themes.*

[📥 Download the themes file](data/r_themes_for_3_sizes.R){.btn .btn-primary download="r_themes_for_3_sizes.R"}

This file defines three theme functions, each built for a different **final printed
size**:

| Function | Built for | Base font |
|-------------------|--------------------------------|-------------------|
| `theme_small()` | \~3 × 3 in — a journal panel | 9 pt |
| `theme_regular()` | \~7 × 7 in — a report figure | 16 pt |
| `theme_large()` | \~16 × 16 in — a poster | 36 pt |

All three give the same publication look: white background, black panel border,
black axis lines and ticks, bold axis titles, no gridlines.

::: callout-important
## Do this once, now

1.  Click the download button above and save `r_themes_for_3_sizes.R` into your
    **project folder** — the same folder your `.Rproj` file is in, *not* inside
    `scripts/`.
2.  Open it in RStudio and **run the whole file**: `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter`
    (or click **Source**).
3.  Look at your **Environment** pane. `theme_small`, `theme_regular`, and
    `theme_large` are now listed under **Functions**. That is all running it does
    — it defines them.
:::

**▶ Run this — from now on, this one line replaces all of it:**

``` r
# ── Part 7b.1 · Source the themes file ──────────────────────────────────
# Put this at the TOP of your script, with your library() lines
source("r_themes_for_3_sizes.R")
```

**▶ Run this — use a theme like any other layer:**

``` r
# ── Part 7b.2 · Use the themes ──────────────────────────────────────────
pine_theme_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 25)) +
  theme_small() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_theme_plot
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Swap `theme_small()` for `theme_regular()` and re-run. What changed?

`______________________________________________________________________________`

::: callout-note
**✅ Why `source()` instead of copy-paste**

`source()` runs that file top to bottom, exactly as if you had typed it. Change a
margin in the themes file once and **every** figure in **every** script picks the
change up the next time you run it. Copy-pasted theme code gives you fifteen
slightly different themes and no way to fix them all.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Watch out!**

`source()` needs the path to be right. With the file in your project root and your
`.Rproj` open, `"r_themes_for_3_sizes.R"` is enough. If you put it in `scripts/`,
the line becomes `source("scripts/r_themes_for_3_sizes.R")`.
:::

# Part 7c · Many plots on one page — `patchwork`

*Follows Lecture Part 7 — `patchwork`.*

**▶ Run this — once per computer:**

``` r
# ── Part 7c.1 · Install patchwork ───────────────────────────────────────
install.packages("patchwork")
```

**▶ Run this — every session, with your other `library()` lines:**

``` r
# ── Part 7c.2 · Load patchwork ──────────────────────────────────────────
library(patchwork)
```

`patchwork` reuses operators you already know: `+` puts plots **side by side**,
`/` puts one **over** the other.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 7c.3 · Combine two plots ───────────────────────────────────────
pine_jitter_plot + pine_mean_se_plot      # side by side

pine_jitter_plot / pine_mean_se_plot      # stacked
```

**▶ Run this — a real three-panel figure:**

``` r
# ── Part 7c.4 · A three-panel figure ────────────────────────────────────
combined_plot <- (pine_jitter_plot + pine_mean_se_plot) / pine_scatter_plot +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

combined_plot
```

Parentheses group plots exactly like arithmetic: `(a + b) / c` puts two panels on
top and one across the bottom. `plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")` tags them
**A**, **B**, **C** — the labels a figure caption refers to.

# Part 8 · Save your figure

*Follows Lecture Part 8 — `ggsave()`.*

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §11 — Communication](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/communication.html), and Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 on what a figure must carry to stand on its own.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 8.1 · Save your figure ─────────────────────────────────────────
# One panel, built with theme_small() — save it at the size that theme was written for
ggsave(
  "figures/pine_needle_boxplot.png",
  plot   = pine_theme_plot,
  width  = 3,
  height = 3,
  units  = "in",
  dpi    = 300
)
```

**▶ Run this — the whole patchwork figure in one call:**

``` r
# ── Part 8.2 · Save the combined figure ─────────────────────────────────
ggsave(
  "figures/pine_needle_combined.png",
  plot   = combined_plot,
  width  = 7,
  height = 6,
  units  = "in",
  dpi    = 300
)
```

A three-panel figure needs roughly three panels' worth of canvas — size `ggsave()`
for the **combined** plot, not for one panel.

Check your `figures/` folder — the PNG should be there.

# Part 8b · Advanced / extra work — `scale_color_manual()`

*Follows Lecture Part 9 — `scale_color_manual()`.*

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §11.4 — Scales](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/communication.html#scales), including the ColorBrewer palettes.

::: callout-tip
**🚀 This part is optional bonus material.** Everything through Part 8 covers the required skills for this module.
:::

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 8b.1 · Advanced / extra work ───────────────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.15), size = 2.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(
    name   = "Side of tree",
    labels = c(shady = "Shady side", sunny = "Sunny side"),
    values = c(shady = "#2c7fb8", sunny = "#d95f0e")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Getting unstuck

When code breaks — and it will, that is normal:

1.  **Read the error message out loud.** R usually names the line and the problem.
2.  **Check the usual suspects:** did you run `library(tidyverse)`? Is `color`/`fill` inside `aes()` when it should be?
3.  `?function_name` opens the built-in help page.
4.  **Bring the exact error** (copy-paste it) to class or office hours.

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §8 — Workflow: getting help](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-help.html).

> 💡 **Key idea:** Every working scientist googles error messages daily. Getting stuck is not failing — it is the job.
